sections.title: 1. Alzheimer's dementia (AD): gross and histological changes

blocks.text: Gross changes in **AD**: diffuse atrophy, flattened cortical sulci and enlarged cerebral ventricles.

Histological changes: neuronal loss (particularly in the cortex and hippocampus), synaptic loss, granulovascular degeneration (small vacuoles with central granules in the cytoplasm of neurons, especially in the temporal lobes), senile plaques, neurofibrillary tangles and Hirano bodies. Astrocytic gliosis and microglial activation are also noted in some cases.

blocks.title: AD: gross vs histological changes
rows: Diffuse atrophy; flattened cortical sulci; enlarged cerebral ventricles
Neuronal loss (cortex, hippocampus); synaptic loss; granulovascular degeneration; senile plaques; neurofibrillary tangles; Hirano bodies

blocks.text: **Q31**: the macroscopic change in **AD** is ventricular enlargement. Neuronal loss, senile plaques, neurofibrillary tangles and vacuolisation are microscopic - do not pick them for a 'macroscopic' stem. The explanation lists the macroscopic changes as enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles, global brain atrophy, reduction in brain weight and sulcal widening.

blocks.subtopic: Protective factors and risk in AD
blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q25** (keyed: apolipoprotein e2 allele) states the e2 allele is a proven protective factor against **AD**; other possible protective factors named in the explanation are smoking, NSAIDs, oestrogen, premorbid intelligence and education.

Not in the notes. **Q20** (keyed: increased tau-to-amyloid ratio in **CSF**) explains early **AD** has reduced **CSF** beta-amyloid and increased **CSF** tau and phosphorylated tau; the **CSF** tau/amyloid beta ratio is nearly 5 times higher in those who later convert to **AD** than in non-converters.

items.text: **Q25**: apolipoprotein e2 allele is the protective factor (options offered Down's syndrome, head injury, post menopausal estrogen decline and age instead); the explanation lists other possible protective factors as smoking, NSAIDs, oestrogen, premorbid intelligence and education.

**Q20**: in mild cognitive impairment the biomarker that detects worsening is an **INCREASED** tau-to-amyloid ratio in **CSF** (early **AD**: reduced **CSF** beta-amyloid, increased **CSF** tau and phosphorylated tau).

Medial temporal atrophy on structural **MRI** is the neuroimaging finding most suggestive of **AD** (grey matter atrophy of hippocampus, entorhinal cortex and amygdala); bilateral pulvinar signal was one of the distractors.

bullets.text: Gross: diffuse atrophy, flattened cortical sulci, enlarged ventricles.
Histology: neuronal loss (cortex, hippocampus), synaptic loss, granulovascular degeneration, plaques, tangles, Hirano bodies.
Astrocytic gliosis and microglial activation only in some cases.
Q31: ventricular enlargement is the macroscopic change; plaques/tangles/neuronal loss are microscopic.

blocks.text: Plaques are insoluble amyloid peptide deposits. The peptide is called Abeta (beta **A4**) peptide. Amyloids are fibrils of multimeric chains of peptides deposited extracellularly, with a beta-pleated sheet conformation.

Abeta is cleaved from a larger transmembrane protein, amyloid-beta precursor protein, by the action of secretases; its formation is prevented by the action of alpha-secretase (the Greek letters are missing in the notes' text; alpha-secretase as the preventing enzyme is confirmed by the **Q19** explanation, which names beta- and gamma-secretase as the ones producing beta amyloid).
Plaques vary in appearance, and two main subtypes are recognised: neuritic and diffuse.

blocks.title: Neuritic vs diffuse plaques
rows: Abeta as amyloid fibrils, among which are irregularly swollen dystrophic neurites (degenerated neuronal processes)
Largely non-fibrillar extracellular Abeta; same peptides as in neuritic plaques but not polymerised to fibrils and lacking beta-sheet configuration
Neurites well visualised with silver stains; may be an eosinophilic mass on H&E; Congo red under polarised light gives 'apple green' birefringence (beta-pleated sheets)
May contain a dense central core of amyloid; microglia and astrocyte processes towards the periphery
Not related to the degree of cognitive decline
Seen in Down syndrome and, to some extent, in normal aging
Yes - only neuritic plaques are counted

blocks.text: **Q19**: the enzyme that prevents amyloid formation is alpha-secretase. Beta-secretase and gamma-secretase processing of amyloid precursor protein is what gives rise to beta amyloid peptide; protein kinase and delta-secretase are distractors.

bullets.text: Plaques = insoluble extracellular Abeta (beta A4) amyloid fibrils, beta-pleated sheet.
Abeta cleaved from APP by beta- and gamma-secretase; alpha-secretase prevents its formation (Q19).
Neuritic plaques: fibrillar amyloid with dystrophic neurites, Congo red apple-green birefringence; seen in Down syndrome and some normal aging.
Diffuse plaques: non-fibrillar Abeta, no beta-sheet, not related to cognitive decline.
Only neuritic plaques are counted in neuropathological tests.

blocks.text: **NFT** are composed of cytoskeletal elements, primarily abnormally phosphorylated tau protein. **AD** is one of the several degenerative tauopathies. Tau is a peptide required for microtubule assembly; microtubules are essential to transport of materials down the axons.

Beta **A4** peptide interacts with cholinergic receptors and this interaction stimulates abnormal phosphorylation of tau. The hyperphosphorylated tau is a major constituent of the tangle and is also present in degenerated neurites, so both tangles and neuritic plaques can be identified by staining with antibody to the abnormal tau.

Most tangles are faintly basophilic; tau immunostaining and silver impregnation improve light microscopic detection. Tangles are mostly intraneuronal, though on neuronal degeneration they may appear extracellularly, thus losing their basophilia.

blocks.title: Spread of tangles and neuropil threads (Love, 2005, as quoted)
columns: Where tangles / neuropil threads are found
rows: Earliest pattern (usually not associated with clinical symptoms)
Restricted to parts of the entorhinal cortex and the **CA1** field of the hippocampus
Increasing density in other parts of the hippocampus and medial temporal neocortex
Other cortical regions and subcortical grey matter structures such as the hypothalamus and thalamus

blocks.text: Braak and Braak (1995) devised a staging scheme, often employed to describe the extent of tangle-related abnormalities (distribution from entorhinal cortex to isocortex) in **AD**; it correlates well with the severity of dementia. Stages V-**VI** operationally define **AD**.

**Q1**: neurofibrillary tangles are made of hyperphosphorylated tau protein (not hypophosphorylated tau, amyloid fibrils, actin filaments or synaptophysin). The explanation adds that hyperphosphorylated tau can self-assemble into tangles of paired helical filaments and straight filaments.

**Q32**: NFTs are most commonly present in the hippocampus in **AD**. The explanation says NFTs also occur with ageing and in the other conditions listed, and are found in the hippocampus (Ammon's horn), amygdala, parahippocampal gyrus, neocortex, locus coeruleus, nucleus of Meynert and raphe nuclei; senile plaques are found in the same sites.

**Q10** (punch drunk syndrome): the keyed neuropathological finding is neurofibrillary tangles (knife blade gyri, basal ganglia enlargement, caudate hypertrophy and pulvinar sign were the distractors) - consistent with **NFT** being listed in dementia pugilistica.

blocks.note: Notes only list **NFT** in dementia pugilistica. **Q10** explanation adds: affects around ==15%== of boxers who suffer concussions after 12-16 years of boxing on average; symptoms develop progressively over a long latent period; histology includes neuronal loss and **NFT**; thinning of the corpus callosum, perforation of the septum pellucidum and ventricular enlargement are also seen.

bullets.text: NFT = abnormally (hyper)phosphorylated tau; AD is a tauopathy; tau is needed for microtubule assembly/axonal transport.
Abeta interacts with cholinergic receptors, stimulating abnormal tau phosphorylation; both tangles and neuritic plaques stain with anti-tau.
NFT also in Down syndrome, dementia pugilistica, Guam parkinson-dementia, Hallervorden-Spatz, normal elderly.
Tangles earliest in entorhinal cortex and CA1 of hippocampus, then medial temporal neocortex, then other cortex and subcortical grey.
Braak staging correlates with dementia severity; stages V-VI define AD.
Q1: tangles = hyperphosphorylated tau.
Q32: tangles most common in the hippocampus in AD.

sections.title: 4. Hirano bodies, cerebral amyloid angiopathy and Binswanger's disease

blocks.text: Hirano bodies are rod-shaped eosinophilic bodies in the cytoplasm of neurons; they are seen in the extracellular space when the neuron dies. They are intracellular aggregates of actin and actin-associated proteins, frequently seen in hippocampal pyramidal cells.

blocks.caption: Boxed note: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) - accumulation of A-beta in the walls of blood vessels (arteries and arterioles) of the cerebral cortex and overlying leptomeninges; about 30% of normal elderly people but over 90% of patients with AD; important cause of (mostly haemorrhagic) strokes in the elderly, superficial lobar haemorrhages that may extend into the subarachnoid space.

blocks.text: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (**CAA**) is the accumulation of Abeta in the walls of blood vessels (particularly arteries and arterioles) in the cerebral cortex and overlying leptomeninges.
**CAA** affects about ==30%== of normal elderly people but over ==90%== of patients with **AD**, in whom the angiopathy also tends to be much more severe.

**CAA** is an important cause of strokes in the elderly, most of them haemorrhagic. Because it is confined to superficial cerebral blood vessels, rupture of amyloid-laden vessels usually causes relatively superficial, lobar haemorrhages that may extend into the subarachnoid space.

blocks.caption: Boxed note: Binswanger's disease - also known as subcortical vascular dementia or subcortical arteriosclerotic encephalopathy; characterized by many small infarctions of the white matter that spare the cortical regions; often coexists with AD-type changes.

blocks.title: Binswanger's disease
rows: Subcortical vascular dementia; subcortical arteriosclerotic encephalopathy
Many small infarctions of the white matter that spare the cortical regions

blocks.text: **Q24**: Hirano bodies in a patient with cognitive impairment point to Alzheimer's dementia (vascular dementia, Wilson disease, **CJD** and Lewy body dementia were distractors).

Hirano bodies in a mock-exam stem: Alzheimer's is keyed (not vascular, Lewy body type, Pick's or frontotemporal). The explanation describes them as intracellular eosinophilic rod-shaped structures in neurons, seen in Alzheimer's and some forms of **CJD**.

blocks.note: Notes do not mention balloon cells. **Q28** (keyed: Pick's disease) states both Hirano bodies and balloon cells are seen together in Pick's disease; Hirano bodies are fusiform or spheroidal eosinophilic bodies commonly seen in the hippocampi of the elderly and numerous in various dementias or degenerative diseases.

blocks.text: **Q28**: when a stem asks for **BOTH** balloon cells and Hirano bodies, Pick's disease is keyed - not Alzheimer's, even though Hirano bodies alone point to **AD** (**Q24**). The explanation says Hirano bodies are numerous in various dementias or degenerative diseases and that both are seen together in Pick's.

blocks.note: Notes cover Binswanger's disease only. **Q6** (keyed: multi-infarct dementia) says arteriosclerotic changes in major arteries are most commonly found in multi-infarct dementia, where multiple cerebral infarcts lead to local or general brain atrophy and ventricular enlargement.

blocks.text: **Q6**: arteriosclerotic changes in major arteries are most commonly found in multi-infarct dementia (not Lewy body dementia, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's disease dementia or normal pressure hydrocephalus); the explanation adds local or general brain atrophy and ventricular enlargement from multiple infarcts.

bullets.text: Hirano bodies: rod-shaped eosinophilic neuronal cytoplasm bodies of actin and actin-associated proteins; frequent in hippocampal pyramidal cells.
CAA = Abeta in walls of cortical/leptomeningeal arteries and arterioles.
CAA in about 30% of normal elderly but over 90% of AD patients (more severe in AD).
CAA: important cause of haemorrhagic stroke; superficial lobar haemorrhage, may reach subarachnoid space.
Binswanger's = subcortical vascular dementia: many small white-matter infarcts sparing cortex; often coexists with AD changes.
Q24: Hirano bodies in a cognitively impaired patient = Alzheimer's.

sections.title: 5. Neuropathological correlates of cognitive decline and hippocampal pathology

blocks.text: The number and distribution of tangles increases as cognitive decline increases. When both neuritic plaques and tangles are present, even a few tangles in a single neocortical field suggest significant cognitive decline.
There is also an association between the numbers of neuritic plaques and the degree of cognitive decline, but it is less apparent than the relationship between tangles and cognitive decline.
The best neuropathological correlate of decline is the number of synapses. The marker for synapses has been antibody to synaptophysin, a protein found in the presynaptic endings.

blocks.title: Relationship of pathological markers to cognitive decline (as stated in the notes)
rows: Associated, but less apparent than for tangles
Not related to the degree of cognitive decline
No simple correlation between number and cognitive decline

blocks.text: Hippocampal pathology: the specific cellular pattern of neuronal loss is in the subiculum of the hippocampal formation and layers **II** and **IV** of the entorhinal cortex.

The affected cells connect the hippocampal formation with the association cortices, basal forebrain, thalamus and hypothalamus (structures crucial to memory). This pattern of neuronal loss isolates the hippocampal formation from its input and output, contributing to the memory disorder in Alzheimer patients.

**Q2**: the pathological factor that correlates most with cognitive decline in **AD** was keyed as burden of neurofibrillary tangles (options also offered diffuse plaques, neuritic plaques, gliosis and vascular amyloid load). The explanation cites Braak staging of tangles, which correlates well with severity of dementia. Do not confuse this with the notes' separate statement that synapse number is the best correlate overall.

bullets.text: Tangle number and distribution rise with cognitive decline; a few neocortical tangles alongside plaques signal significant decline.
Neuritic plaque association with decline is less apparent than for tangles.
Best neuropathological correlate = number of synapses (synaptophysin antibody marker).
Neuronal loss in subiculum and entorhinal layers II and IV isolates hippocampal formation from input/output - memory disorder.
Q2: keyed answer tangle burden (Braak staging).

blocks.text: Lewy bodies are weakly eosinophilic, spherical, cytoplasmic inclusions.

blocks.title: Lewy body distribution: Parkinson's disease vs DLB
rows: Also in many areas of the cerebrum: temporal lobe, cingulate gyrus, frontal lobes; may also be found in the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

blocks.text: A 5-year Parkinson's disease history with cognitive decline, visual hallucinations and alpha-synuclein deposits points to Lewy bodies (not Pick cells, tau proteins, Hirano bodies or Pick bodies). The explanation says Lewy bodies are confined to the substantia nigra in Parkinson's disease, and that Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia are classed as synucleinopathies.

Cortical Lewy bodies are less conspicuous, less eosinophilic and lack a clear halo compared with those in the substantia nigra; they take up a homogeneous eosinophilic staining in the cytoplasm with peripheral displacement of the nucleus.
There is no simple correlation between the number of Lewy bodies and cognitive decline. An antibody to ubiquitin (written 'protease ubiquitin' in the notes) can be used to identify Lewy bodies.

Lewy bodies in Parkinson's disease and **DLB** contain accumulations of alpha-synuclein; staining with alpha-synuclein antibodies is an excellent tool for detecting them. **DLB** is one of the degenerative synucleopathies.
Alpha-synuclein accelerates reuptake of dopamine in neurons, and this dopamine overload might be toxic.

blocks.caption: Two-column coloured table: Tauopathies (tau deposits) - Alzheimer's dementia, Pick's disease, Progressive supranuclear palsy, Corticobasal degenerations, Frontotemporal dementia with parkinsonism (FTDP-17); Synucleopathies (alpha synuclein deposits) - Parkinson's, DLB, Multisystem atrophy.

blocks.text: A high proportion of patients with **DLB**/**PDD** (about ==75%==) also have **AD**-type neuropathological abnormalities, though the plaque/tangle burden associated with dementia is less than that seen in Alzheimer's disease.

Lewy neurites are nerve cell processes containing aggregates of alpha-synuclein. They can occur in both **DLB**/dementia of Parkinson's disease and idiopathic Parkinson's disease and are most numerous in the **CA2**/3 region of the hippocampus and in the substantia nigra.
Some patients with **DLB** show microvacuolation of the cerebral cortex, predominantly in the medial temporal regions. This can mimic a prion disease.

**Q30**: an elderly man with marked tremor, progressive cognitive decline and tau-**NEGATIVE** cells at autopsy is Lewy body dementia (not Alzheimer's dementia, frontal lobe degeneration, vascular dementia or **CJD**). The explanation says Lewy bodies rarely have tau deposits and are primarily alpha synuclein and ubiquitin.

items.text: **Q7**: alpha-synuclein is a major constituent of Lewy bodies (not neurofibrillary tangles, Pick's bodies, prion particles or neuritic plaques).

**Q16**: Lewy bodies contain alpha-synuclein; the explanation adds ubiquitin, protein neurofilaments, granular material, dense core vesicles and microtubule assembly protein, and says density is much higher in the cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus and temporal cortex in Lewy body dementia.

The body made of ubiquitin and alpha synuclein, associated with loss of dopaminergic neurons in the basal ganglia, is the Lewy body (not Hirano bodies, neurofibrillary tangles, Barr bodies or prion bodies).

blocks.subtopic: Parkinson's disease macroscopic and histological changes
blocks.note: Not in the notes beyond Lewy body location. **Q26** (keyed: Parkinson's disease) says macroscopic changes include depigmentation of the substantia nigra (particularly the zona compacta) and locus coeruleus and diffuse cortical atrophy; histology includes reactive astrocytosis, neuronal loss and Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra, locus coeruleus, dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, hypothalamus, nucleus basalis of Meynert, Edinger-Westphal nucleus and raphe nuclei.

blocks.text: **Q26**: depigmentation of the substantia nigra = Parkinson's disease (not **CJD**, Huntington's, Dandy-Walker malformation or Alzheimer's). The explanation specifies the zona compacta, adds depigmentation of the locus coeruleus and diffuse cortical atrophy, and lists Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra, locus coeruleus, dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, hypothalamus, nucleus basalis of Meynert, Edinger-Westphal nucleus and raphe nuclei.

bullets.text: Lewy bodies: weakly eosinophilic spherical cytoplasmic inclusions containing alpha-synuclein (and detectable by ubiquitin antibody).
PD: Lewy bodies confined to substantia nigra; DLB: also temporal, cingulate, frontal cortex (+ dorsal motor nucleus of vagus).
Cortical Lewy bodies: less conspicuous, less eosinophilic, no clear halo.
No simple correlation between Lewy body number and cognitive decline.
Tauopathies: AD, Pick's, PSP, corticobasal, FTDP-17. Synucleopathies: Parkinson's, DLB, multisystem atrophy.
About 75% of DLB/PDD also have AD-type changes (lower plaque/tangle burden); microvacuolation can mimic prion disease.
Q30: tau-negative cells + tremor + cognitive decline = Lewy body dementia.

facts.label: Proportion of DLB/PDD with AD-type abnormalities

blocks.text: **FTD** is associated with three types of underlying pathology: frontal lobe degeneration type, Pick's type and motor neurone disease (**MND**) type.

blocks.title: Three pathological types of FTD
rows: Most common type; spongiform degeneration/microvacuolation of superficial neuropil chiefly in layers **III** and V of the cortex; loss of large cortical nerve cells with minimal gliosis
Preponderance of atrophy in frontotemporal regions; loss of large cortical nerve cells, abundant gliosis and neuronal Pick's bodies (masses of cytoskeletal elements)

Cerebral atrophy less marked, limbic areas largely preserved; loss of large cortical nerve cells, microvacuolation and mild gliosis; ubiquitinated but not tau-immunoreactive inclusions in frontal cortex and hippocampus; **MND** pathology also in anterior horn cells

blocks.text: **FTD** vignette (75-year-old, memory problems, disinhibition, lack of insight): the keyed microscopic finding is cytoplasmic inclusions - not spongiform encephalopathy, intraneuronal inclusions or beta amyloid peptides. The explanation says tau-positive inclusions account for most cases, while the other main finding is ubiquitin-only pathology with cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions (negative for tau or alpha-synuclein), suggesting a link with **ALS**.
Pick cells are abnormal swollen oval-shaped neuronal cells with loss of Nissl's substance and a peripherally displaced nucleus.

Pick's bodies are seen in some postmortem specimens but are not necessary for the diagnosis. They are argentophilic, tau and ubiquitin reactive filamentous inclusions. Hirano bodies may also be seen, with lesser frequency than in Alzheimer's.

blocks.caption: Boxed note: Huntington's dementia - severe loss of small neurons in the caudate and putamen with subsequent astrocytosis; characteristic protein deposits form nuclear inclusions in neurons of HD patients; head of the caudate becomes shrunken with 'ex vacuo' dilatation of the anterior horns of the lateral ventricles.

blocks.title: Huntington's dementia (side box in the notes)
rows: Severe loss of small neurons in the caudate and putamen, with subsequent astrocytosis
Characteristic protein deposits form nuclear inclusions in neurons
Head of the caudate becomes shrunken; 'ex vacuo' dilatation of the anterior horns of the lateral ventricles

expansion: Marked atrophy of the corpus striatum, particularly the caudate nucleus
Marked atrophy of the cerebral cortex, particularly the frontal lobe gyri
Dilatation of the lateral and third ventricles

blocks.text: Atrophy of the head of the caudate on **CT** = Huntington's disease (not Alzheimer's, Wilson's, Fahr's or Pick's). The explanation says this is characteristic especially in late stages, and that in Fahr's disease calcified basal ganglia are noted instead.

blocks.note: The term 'knife blade' is not in the notes. **Q12** (keyed: Pick's disease) defines knife-blade atrophy as marked atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes with relative sparing of parietal and occipital lobes in Pick's disease.

blocks.text: **Q12**: knife-blade atrophy = Pick's disease (not Alzheimer's, Lewy body dementia, **CJD** or progressive supranuclear palsy): marked atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes with relative sparing of the parietal and occipital lobes.

items.text: **Q29**: the immunological staining for Pick's disease is anti-tau antibodies; the explanation says anti-tau and anti-ubiquitin immunohistochemistry is the most efficient and highly specific method, whereas the tangles of Alzheimer's stain with antibodies to basic fibroblast growth factor, amyloid P and heparan sulfate glycosaminoglycan.

**Q15**: marked atrophy of the caudate nucleus = Huntington's disease (not punch drunk syndrome, alcoholic dementia, **CJD** or Lewy body dementia); the explanation adds marked atrophy of the corpus striatum, small brain, frontal cortical atrophy and dilatation of the lateral and third ventricles.

**Q17**: knife blade gyri are more likely in Pick's than other dementias (ventricular **SHRINKAGE** is wrong - ventricles enlarge); Pick bodies are round argyrophilic intraneuronal inclusions and Pick cells are swollen cortical pyramidal cells.

bullets.text: FTD has three pathological types: frontal lobe degeneration (most common), Pick's, MND type.
Frontal lobe type: microvacuolation in layers III and V; loss of large cortical neurons, minimal gliosis.
Pick's type: frontotemporal atrophy, abundant gliosis, Pick's bodies (tau- and ubiquitin-reactive, argentophilic; not necessary for diagnosis); Pick cells swollen with displaced nucleus.
MND type: less atrophy, limbic areas preserved, ubiquitinated but tau-negative inclusions, anterior horn cell pathology.
Huntington's: severe small-neuron loss in caudate and putamen, nuclear inclusions, shrunken caudate head with ex vacuo dilatation of anterior horns.
Q29: Pick's disease stained with anti-tau antibodies.
FTD microscopy: tau-positive inclusions in most cases; otherwise ubiquitin-only cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions (linked to ALS).

blocks.text: Three forms exist: sporadic (most common), familial and variant **CJD** (vCJD, related to bovine spongiform encephalopathy).
There are no characteristic gross pathologic features because of the typically short course; persons living beyond 6 months to a year may have some generalized cerebral atrophy.

Microscopically **CJD** shows spongiform encephalopathy secondary to neuropil vacuolisation: many round to oval vacuoles in the neuropil of cortical gray matter, single or multiloculated, which may coalesce to microcysts. Most cases also show neuronal loss and gliosis.

Prion protein (PrPc) is a normal neuronal cell surface protein encoded by a gene on chromosome 20. In **CJD** it is converted by a conformational change to an abnormal, protease-resistant form, PrPSc, which accumulates in the **CNS** and triggers further conversion of PrPc to PrPSc, accounting for the degenerative changes in the cerebral cortex. PrP can be identified in tissues with immunoperoxidase staining.
PrPSc can be transmitted from one person with spongiform encephalopathy to another via pituitary extracts, corneal transplants, dural grafts and contaminated electrodes from neurosurgical procedures.

blocks.caption: Table: Feature / Classic CJD / Variant CJD, rows Age, Course, Symptoms, EEG, MRI, Biopsy, Tonsils (coloured header).

blocks.title: Classic CJD vs variant CJD
rows: Early psychiatric/behavioural signs with delayed neurological features
Triphasic waves rare; changes often non-specific
Prion protein cannot be isolated from lymphoid tissue

blocks.text: **Q23**: the keyed difference between **CJD** and vCJD is **EARLIER** **AGE** **OF** **ONSET** (average age of death 29 years; death on average within 14 months). Earlier onset of ataxia, negative tonsillar biopsy, absence of florid plaques and typical **EEG** changes were the wrong options.
In variant **CJD** there is a marked accumulation of prion protein and the plaques are florid.

An abnormal protein, 14-3-3, can be found in the **CSF** by immunoassay, but it is non-specific and may be found with viral encephalitis and stroke; it is less frequent in variant **CJD**. In familial **CJD** the typical **EEG** changes are often lacking and 14-3-3 is absent in **CSF** in more than ==50%== of cases.

blocks.title: Codon 129 polymorphism of PrP (methionine M / valine V)

blocks.text: **MRI** is the most useful supportive diagnostic test in variant **CJD**. The pulvinar sign (posterior thalamic region abnormality) is highly sensitive and specific for vCJD and was found in more than ==90%== of pathologically proven vCJD cases; **FLAIR** sequences are most likely to show it.

Increased signal in the pulvinar nucleus of the thalamus bilaterally is the neuroimaging finding most suggestive of new variant **CJD** (not medial temporal atrophy on structural **MRI**, occipital hypoperfusion on **HMPAO-SPECT** or impaired dorsolateral cortex function). The explanation says **MRI** is the most useful supportive test and the pulvinar sign is highly sensitive and specific for vCJD.

In **CJD** amyloid plaques are prominent in the cerebellum (not raphe nuclei, corpus callosum, occipital cortex or hippocampus); the explanation calls **CJD** a multifocal dementia involving cerebellar structures.

blocks.subtopic: Variant CJD age and survival figures
blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q23** explanation: vCJD was first reported in 1996, affects younger people than other forms, average age of death 29 years, death on average within 14 months.

Notes say there are no characteristic gross features. **Q13** (keyed: **CJD**, for selective cerebellar atrophy) says macroscopic changes would include generalised cerebral atrophy, sometimes selective cerebellar atrophy, and ventricular enlargement; histology: status spongiosus, neuronal degeneration without inflammation and astrocytic proliferation.

blocks.text: **Q13**: selective cerebellar atrophy points to **CJD** (not Lewy body dementia, Alzheimer's, normal pressure hydrocephalus or Parkinson's disease dementia). The explanation: generalised cerebral atrophy, sometimes selective cerebellar atrophy and ventricular enlargement; histology of status spongiosus, neuronal degeneration **WITHOUT** inflammation, astrocytic proliferation, nerve cell loss and gliosis.

items.text: **Q4**: a 33-year-old with anxiety/depression, then rapidly progressive cognitive impairment, myoclonus, ataxia and akinetic mutism = **CJD**; characteristic autopsy change is extensive vacuole formation (not Lewy bodies or lack of gliosis).
Mock stem 'what accounts for the spongiform appearance in **CJD**': neuronal vacuolation is keyed (not accumulation of prion proteins, trapped air, neuronal loss or neuropil loss).

bullets.text: Forms: sporadic (most common), familial, variant (BSE-related).
Histology: spongiform change from neuropil vacuolation, neuronal loss and gliosis; no characteristic gross change.
PrPc (chromosome 20) converts to protease-resistant PrPSc, which propagates conversion.
Transmission via pituitary extracts, corneal transplants, dural grafts, neurosurgical electrodes.
vCJD vs classic: younger (3rd/4th decade), longer course (1 year vs 5 months), psychiatric onset, pulvinar sign, many plaques, tonsils positive.
Codon 129 M/M: 37% healthy, 73% sporadic CJD, 100% vCJD.
Pulvinar sign on MRI (FLAIR): over 90% of proven vCJD; 14-3-3 non-specific and less frequent in vCJD.
vCJD: pulvinar sign (bilateral pulvinar signal on MRI) is highly sensitive and specific.

blocks.text: The notes state the major **HIV-1** receptors are **CD4** and **CD8**, with chemokine receptors such as **CXCR4** and **CCR5** as co-receptors. **CD4**+ helper T lymphocytes are the major route of multiplication and entry, apart from monocytes; infected **CD4**+ T cells and monocytes circulating in blood are the potential source of **CNS** infection.

Strains isolated from the brain infect macrophages rather than lymphocytes. Macrophage tropism is related to a mutation in a specific region of gp120, the external glycoprotein of the virus; in late infection active replication generates more of these mutants and the compromised immune system lets them escape, so macrophage-tropic strains predominate.

blocks.title: How HIV-1 enters the CNS
rows: **HIV** enters the **CNS** as a passenger in cells trafficking to the brain (**CD4** T cells or monocytes); virus accumulation in perivascular regions is proof for the model
Entry of free **HIV-1** by migration between, or transcytosis of, endothelial cells; mechanism of endothelial infection is controversial as **CD4** expression in endothelial cells is unclear

blocks.text: In order to enter the brain **HIV-1** must cross the **BBB** by mechanisms that remain unclear.

All main **CNS** cell types (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, neurons, perivascular macrophages, microglia) could theoretically be infected, but only perivascular macrophages and microglia are the most commonly infected. Most studies indicate absence of in vivo infection in neurons.
Mechanism of neuropathogenesis has two components: (1) the direct effect of **HIV-1** infection and (2) the indirect consequence of infection, comprising secretion of cytokines and neurotoxins.

Infected macrophages and microglia participate in neurodegeneration by shedding viral proteins and releasing cytokines and neurotoxins into the **CNS**. Tat and **TNF**-alpha contribute to disruption of the blood-brain barrier, which becomes more permeable to infected monocytes and peripheral cytokines.

Secreted pro-inflammatory cytokines activate microglia and astrocytes, which secrete neurotoxins; altered astrocyte function further increases neurotoxicity. Neuronal injury via apoptosis is currently believed to be produced by toxic products released directly by **HIV**-infected macrophages and microglia or by activated astrocytes.

blocks.title: Neurotoxic factors identified
rows: Toxic for oligodendrocytes and can cause demyelination

blocks.title: Biopsy findings in HIV-infected brain tissue
rows: Multinucleated giant cells from virus-induced fusion of microglia and/or macrophages in central white and deep gray matter
Neuronal loss, particularly in hippocampus, basal ganglia and caudate nucleus
Variable degree of white matter pathology with myelin damage
Accumulation of lipid macrophages in extreme cases

blocks.caption: Boxed note: VIRAL LOAD - current method used to predict stage of disease, monitor progression and formulate treatment is viral load (viral particles per cubic millimetre of blood); HIV-1 can also be detected in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), but CSF viral load is not established as an accurate indicator of CNS disease related to HIV.

blocks.text: Viral load (the actual number of viral particles in a cubic millimeter of blood) is the current method used to predict stage of disease, monitor progression and formulate treatment strategies. **HIV-1** can also be detected in **CSF**, but **CSF** viral load is not established as an accurate indicator of **CNS** disease related to **HIV**.
The most common psychiatric presentation in **AIDS** is **HIV**-related dementia, followed by depression. Psychosis is seen in only ==10%== of **HIV**-infected individuals.

**Q18**: the true statement is that **HIV** crosses the blood brain barrier using macrophages (Trojan Horse hypothesis, via **CD4** T cells or monocytes). The distractors are wrong: psychosis is **NOT** the most common **HIV** psychiatric problem, **CSF** viral load is **NOT** the best predictor of **CNS** disease, and **HIV** neuronal injury does occur via apoptosis.

An **IV** heroin user with significant slowing of cognition, fatuous affect and impaired concentration of insidious onset: **HIV** dementia is keyed (not opioid intoxication, heroin withdrawal, bacterial encephalitis or depression).

blocks.subtopic: HIV dementia in an IV drug user
blocks.note: **Q22** (keyed: **HIV** dementia) explains intravenous drug use is a common source of **HIV** infection and that subcortical dementia is common in **HIV** patients in the late stages of illness; the notes do not mention subcortical dementia.

bullets.text: CD4+ T cells and monocytes are the route of entry; brain strains are macrophage-tropic (gp120 mutation).
Trojan Horse hypothesis: HIV crosses the BBB inside CD4 T cells/monocytes; alternative = free virus via endothelium.
Perivascular macrophages and microglia are the most commonly infected CNS cells; neurons not infected in vivo.
Neuropathogenesis: direct effect plus indirect cytokine/neurotoxin effect; Tat and TNF-alpha open the BBB.
Neurotoxins: platelet activating factor, quinolinic acid, nitric oxide, arachidonic acid metabolites; TNF demyelinates.
Biopsy: macrophage infiltration, microglial nodules, multinucleated giant cells, astrocyte damage, neuronal loss, myelin damage.
CSF viral load is not an accurate indicator of CNS disease; most common psychiatric presentation is dementia, then depression; psychosis only 10%.

facts.label: Most common psychiatric presentation in AIDS

blocks.title: Gross changes in schizophrenia
rows: Decrease in brain weight, brain length and volume of the cerebral hemispheres
Enlargement of the lateral ventricles (especially temporal horns)
Thalamus; temporolimbic structures including hippocampus, amygdala, parahippocampal gyrus
Reductions in parahippocampal gyrus or hippocampus
Increased incidence of cavum septi pellucidi

blocks.text: Basal ganglia volume reduction was noted especially in the preneuroleptic era, in the catatonic subgroup. Enlargement of basal ganglia is now more common as a consequence of treatment with classical neuroleptics, and can be reversed by atypical substances.
Schizophrenia-like psychosis is commoner in temporal lobe epilepsy when the focus is in the left hemisphere.

The planum temporale, the posterior superior surface of the superior temporal gyrus, is a highly lateralized brain structure involved with language. In schizophrenic patients a consistent reversal of the normal left-larger-than-right asymmetry of planum temporale surface area is noted. Heschl's gyrus (primary auditory cortex) showed no differences between the left and right sides.

**Q9**: the planum temporale is normally larger on the **LEFT**. The distractor 'in schizophrenia left more than right asymmetry is noted' is wrong: schizophrenia shows a consistent **REVERSAL** of the normal left-larger-than-right asymmetry.

Histology: no evidence for astrogliosis. Reduced cell numbers or size has been described, especially of neurons in the hippocampus and **DLPFC**; increased neuronal density, possibly relating to decreased neuronal size (decreased dendritic arborization and neuropil), has been reported.

Least likely in schizophrenia = gliosis: no evidence for astrogliosis has been reported. Increased neuronal density (possibly relating to smaller neurons), cytoarchitectural anomalies, reduced cell size and reduced cell number (hippocampus, **DLPFC**) **ARE** described.
Subtle cytoarchitectural anomalies are described in the hippocampal formation and frontal cortex, e.g. significant cellular disarray at the **CA3-CA4** interface.

Synaptic studies in the hippocampus and **DLPFC** show decrements in presynaptic markers, which may reflect fewer synaptic contacts and support the hypothesis of excessive synaptic pruning. Glutamatergic synapses may be especially vulnerable in the hippocampus and perhaps **DLPFC**, with predominantly GABAergic involvement in the cingulate gyrus.
Antipsychotics alter synaptic and neuronal morphology, particularly in the caudate-putamen, and may increase glial density in the prefrontal cortex.

blocks.subtopic: Handedness and sex effect on planum temporale asymmetry
blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q5** explanation: the leftward volume asymmetry is related to the degree of right-handedness and is more marked in males (nearly ten times asymmetrical on the left in males).

blocks.text: **Q5**: in healthy right-handed subjects the planum temporale is larger on the left (not cingulate cortex, superior colliculus, thalamus or amygdala); the leftward asymmetry relates to the degree of right-handedness and is more marked in males.

bullets.text: Gross: reduced brain weight/volume, enlarged lateral ventricles (temporal horns), reduced thalamic and temporolimbic volume, cavum septi pellucidi.
Basal ganglia enlargement now follows classical neuroleptics (reversible with atypicals).
Planum temporale: normal left>right asymmetry is reversed in schizophrenia; Heschl's gyrus unaffected.
Histology: no astrogliosis; reduced neuronal size/number in hippocampus and DLPFC; disarray at CA3-CA4.
Reduced presynaptic markers support excessive synaptic pruning; glutamatergic (hippocampus/DLPFC) and GABAergic (cingulate) synapses implicated.
Q9: planum temporale normally larger on the left.
Gliosis is the finding least likely in schizophrenia (no astrogliosis reported).

blocks.text: A strong association between mood disorder and the number and severity of focal signal hyperintensities on **T2**-weighted images has been established. These white matter hyperintensities (**WMH**) occur particularly in the deep subcortical white matter and to a lesser extent in the basal ganglia and periventricular tissue.
**WMH** are seen in excess in both bipolar and unipolar mood disorder, with an odds ratio of 3 to 7 compared with healthy controls.

In major depression, **WMH** are particularly common in elderly subjects, where they are linked to risk factors for, and the presence of, vascular disease. **WMH** confer a poor prognosis in major depression and bipolar disorder.
**Lithium** treatment increases cortical grey matter volume, suggesting **lithium** is neurotrophic; it may also enhance neurogenesis and inhibit apoptosis.
Antidepressants may affect neuronal morphology: in animal models they help regenerate monoaminergic axons, promote hippocampal neurogenesis and prevent loss of dendritic spines.

**Q11**: white matter hyperintensities in mood disorders are associated with vascular risk factors. Distractors that are wrong: best seen on **T1** images (they are seen on **T2**-weighted images), seen only in bipolar (seen in both bipolar and unipolar), good recovery (they confer poor prognosis), more often in younger patients (more common in the elderly).

bullets.text: WMH on T2-weighted MRI: deep subcortical white matter, less in basal ganglia/periventricular tissue.
In excess in both bipolar and unipolar disorder (odds ratio 3 to 7).
In elderly depression linked to vascular disease; WMH confer poor prognosis.
Lithium increases cortical grey matter (neurotrophic); antidepressants promote hippocampal neurogenesis in animal models.
Q11: WMH associated with vascular risk factors.

facts.label: WMH odds ratio vs healthy controls

blocks.text: Wernicke's encephalopathy is characterized by degenerative changes including gliosis and small haemorrhages in structures surrounding the third ventricle and aqueduct (mamillary bodies, hypothalamus, mediodorsal thalamic nucleus, colliculi, midbrain tegmentum), as well as cerebellar atrophy.
Brain shrinkage can be found in uncomplicated alcoholism, largely accounted for by loss of white matter; some of this damage appears reversible.

Alcohol-related neuronal loss has been documented in specific regions of the cerebral cortex (superior frontal association cortex), the hypothalamus (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei) and the cerebellum.

**Q14**: a binge-drinking 55-year-old with new-learning deficits (retains messages long enough to converse) - the most prominent pathology is in the dorsal medial thalamus (mediodorsal thalamic nucleus), not the hippocampus, **DLPFC**, hypothalamus or cerebellum.

bullets.text: Wernicke's: gliosis and small haemorrhages around third ventricle/aqueduct (mamillary bodies, hypothalamus, mediodorsal thalamus, colliculi, tegmentum) plus cerebellar atrophy.
Uncomplicated alcoholism: brain shrinkage from white matter loss, partly reversible.
Neuronal loss: superior frontal association cortex, hypothalamic supraoptic/paraventricular nuclei, cerebellum.
Q14: mediodorsal (dorsal medial) thalamus.

blocks.text: Hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis and, to some extent, the cerebellar hemispheres is documented.
Purkinje cell count in the cerebellum is significantly lower.
Changes in the neocortex are inconsistent. Some suggest increased cortical volume, probably related to reduced pruning.

**Q3**: a child with challenging behaviour and stereotyped motor activity - the **MRI** finding associated with autism is hypoplastic cerebellum (not cerebral atrophy, medial temporal atrophy, caudate atrophy or white matter hyperintensities).

Autism vignette (12-year-old, reduced social interaction, poor communication, repetitive stereotyped behaviour): hypoplasia of the **CEREBELLAR** **VERMIS** is keyed (not hippocampus, fusiform gyrus, amygdala or angular gyrus); the hemispheres are involved only 'to some extent' and Purkinje cell count is lower.

bullets.text: Cerebellar vermis (and partly hemispheres) hypoplasia.
Cerebellar Purkinje cell count significantly lower.
Neocortical changes inconsistent; possibly increased volume from reduced pruning.
Q3: hypoplastic cerebellum.

blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q8** (keyed: multiple sclerosis) explains **EAE** is a laboratory model used to study the efficacy of potential agents treating **MS**, and to investigate the pathogenesis of autoimmunity, **CNS** inflammation and demyelination.

Not in the notes. **Q21** (keyed: loss of memory of personal events well rehearsed) says this is characteristic of dissociative amnesia: well rehearsed personal events are lost (e.g. that her husband was ill before death).

Not in the notes. A 37-year-old with waxing and waning neurological deficits has multiple sclerosis; the keyed pathological change is demyelination (gradual demyelination delays and inhibits signal conduction). Gliosis, Lewy bodies, neuritic plaques and amyloid plaques were distractors.

Not in the notes. Newborn with seizures, hydrocephalus, midline facial anomaly, spasticity and agenesis of the corpus callosum: the keyed underlying pathology is a disorder of neuronal migration (not obstetric tissue loss, congenital infection, excessive synaptic pruning or neurodegeneration).

Not in the notes. The exception keyed was Epstein Barr virus: **EBV** (infectious mononucleosis) has not been implicated in learning disability syndromes; **CMV**, toxoplasmosis, Treponema pallidum and rubella were the other options. Measles (rubeola), unlike German measles (rubella), does not cause congenital anomalies/learning disabilities.

Not in the notes. Viral encephalitis with increased oral exploratory behaviour and inappropriate sexuality = Kluver-Bucy syndrome: hypermetamorphopsia (compulsion to attend to all visual stimuli), hyperorality, hypersexuality and blunted emotional reactivity. The full syndrome is rarely seen in man, but a partial syndrome can occur with viral encephalitis affecting the temporal lobe.

Not in the notes. Kuru has the slowest course among the options (sporadic, variant and iatrogenic **CJD**, Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker syndrome): incubation up to 40 years before onset, then rapid and fatal; thought to be transmitted by ritual cannibalism; symptoms include personality and behavioural disturbances, progressive cerebellar ataxia, dementia and death.

Not in the notes. In a 55-year-old with leg and hand weakness, tongue fasciculations and memory deficits diagnosed as **ALS**, the primary pathological change is in motor neurons (not neuromuscular junction, myocytes, spinal autonomic ganglion or sensory neurons); the explanation says upper motor neurons are specifically damaged, with loss of cells in anterior horns of cord and brainstem nuclei.

bullets.text: EAE is a lab model for studying MS treatments, autoimmunity, CNS inflammation and demyelination (Q8).
Dissociative amnesia: well rehearsed personal events lost (Q21).
Waxing/waning neurological deficits = MS; pathology is demyelination (mock-exam stem).
Agenesis of corpus callosum = disorder of neuronal migration (mock-exam stem).
EBV is not implicated in learning disability; measles unlike rubella causes no congenital anomalies (mock-exam stem).
Kluver-Bucy: hypermetamorphopsia, hyperorality, hypersexuality, blunted emotion; partial form in temporal-lobe viral encephalitis (mock-exam stem).
Kuru: slowest prion course (incubation up to 40 years), ritual cannibalism, cerebellar ataxia, dementia (mock-exam stem).
ALS: primary pathology in motor neurons (anterior horn cells, brainstem nuclei) (mock-exam stem).
